Meta Just Dropped 9% in a Week. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©Photodjo from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Meta stock fell about 9% in the past week (through Friday's close). Most of the drop came after a third-quarter report that showed 26% revenue growth and negative free cash flow.

The ad business is still growing fast, and the selling is about how Meta pays for AI, including a new non-voting Class C stock that is partly for raising capital.

A $25 billion New Mexico fine adds to the quarter's $9.89 billion legal charge, though Meta's cash covers the fine several times over.

After the drop, Meta trades below its usual forward multiple, which makes it a buy for investors who can live with some dilution.

Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) is down about 9% over the past week (through Friday's close). Most of that came after a third-quarter report that was strong everywhere except cash. (The Nasdaq 100 fell just 2%.)

Ads grew 26%, and that wasn't enough

Revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, ahead of the $63.41 billion analysts expected. Without a $9.89 billion legal charge, earnings per share would have been $7.40, against $6.80 expected. And fourth-quarter guidance of $73 billion to $76 billion has a midpoint above consensus.

But CFO Susan Li gave no 2027 budget. She said Meta plans "to continue investing aggressively to support both our core business and emerging AI initiatives."

The AI bill is coming due

Third-quarter capex hit $34.91 billion, above the $32.79 billion of operating cash flow. That left free cash flow at negative $2.12 billion. It's been building for years: capex took about 60% of operating cash flow in 2025, up from 32% in 2021…

Meta Platforms (META): cash from operations vs. capital expenditures, $ billions, fiscal 2021–2025 (TIKR)

…and Meta just raised the floor of its 2026 capex range to $135 billion. On top of that, Meta had $454.5 billion of non-cancelable contractual commitments as of Sept. 30.

Then there's a new non-voting Class C stock, arriving in January 2027. It's partly for raising capital. Meta has looked like the AI spender that doesn't need outside money, unlike OpenAI. If it does sell new shares, the spending has to earn its keep. And on Thursday, Meta's credit default swaps hit a record high.

Another $25 billion legal bill

Plus: the day Meta reported, a New Mexico court ordered it to pay $25 billion over the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Interest runs at 15% a year. Meta says it will win on appeal. Even if it doesn't, its $82.5 billion of cash covers the fine more than three times over.

title: What Is Meta Platforms (META) Telling Investors With Its Sundial Deal And New Stock?

What Is Meta Platforms (META) Telling Investors With Its Sundial Deal And New Stock?
Bailey Pemberton

META

Meta Platforms (NasdaqGS:META) agreed to acquire AI data analytics platform Sundial, aiming to deepen its data-focused AI toolset.

The company introduced a new nonvoting stock structure intended to address potential liabilities from a proposed California wealth tax on Mark Zuckerberg.

Meta indicated that the nonvoting share class is designed so Zuckerberg can meet tax obligations without reducing his voting control over the business.

The Sundial acquisition and new nonvoting stock both matter, but Meta's broader story runs well beyond this twin move. Check out 1 major warning sign that Meta Platforms investors should know about.

For readers looking at how AI infrastructure could shape the next phase of platforms like Meta, the next stop is 55 AI infrastructure stocks.

NasdaqGS:META Earnings & Revenue Growth as at Oct 2026

Meta Platforms now runs a US$1.6t interactive media and services operation that spans social apps, VR headsets, and AI glasses, so a move deeper into AI data analytics and capital structure tweaks directly influences how its products are built and financed globally.

3 things going right for Meta Platforms that this headline doesn't cover.

How does Sundial fit into Meta Platforms' AI push?

Sundial plugs directly into Meta Platforms' heavy AI infrastructure build by giving product teams faster ways to query data with natural language and chat style interfaces. That can tighten the loop between user behavior, model training and ad or product tweaks. For investors, the key link is whether these tools help Meta do more with the US$130b to US$145b of 2026 AI capex already on the table.

Does this Sundial deal and nonvoting stock change the Meta Platforms narrative?

The acquisition leans into the narrative catalyst that AI driven ad performance and business messaging are supporting stronger revenue, while the new Class C nonvoting shares speak directly to governance and regulatory risk. Structuring Zuckerberg's wealth tax planning around nonvoting stock ties founder control more tightly to the very high AI spend that could pressure free cash flow if returns fall short.

See how these catalysts shape Meta Platforms' path to a $814 fair value.

What should investors watch next to judge whether this pays off for Meta?

The next real test is how often management starts citing Sundial style AI analytics on earnings calls in 2027 when explaining ad conversion gains, engagement metrics or AI agent usage. If those datapoints become regular, it will show whether this data stack is truly becoming a core driver of Meta Platforms' results rather than just a side project.

title: Cathie Wood buys $24.5 million of tumbling megacap stock

Cathie Wood buys $24.5 million of tumbling megacap stock
Silin Chen, Celine Provini
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 10:07 AM PDT 7 min read
ARKK
META
^GSPC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Cathie Wood, chief of Ark Investment Management, often buys her favorite tech stocks when their prices fall.

That's what she's doing with Meta Platforms (META), adding shares after the Facebook parent's stock tumbled following its earnings report.

Last year, the flagship Ark Innovation ETF gained 35.49%, far outpacing the S&P 500's return of 17.88% in the same period. So far this year, Wood's flagship Ark Innovation ETF (ARKK) is up 6.59% as of Oct. 23, while the S&P 500 surged 11.37%.

Wood gained a reputation after the Ark Innovation ETF delivered a rosy 153% return in 2020. But her style also brings painful losses in bearish markets, as seen in 2022, when the ETF tumbled more than 60%.

Those swings have weighed on Wood's long-term gains. As of Oct. 23, her Ark Innovation ETF has delivered a five-year annualized return of -6.83%, while the S&P 500 has an annualized return of 10.9% over the same period, according to data from Morningstar.

Cathie Wood remains optimistic about AI and tech revolution

Wood focuses on high-tech companies across artificial intelligence, blockchain, biomedical technology, and robotics. She believes these businesses have strong growth potential, but their volatility often causes fluctuations in the Ark's funds.

Over the decade ended 2025, the Ark Innovation ETF wiped out nearly $5 billion in investor wealth, according to a report by Morningstar's analyst Amy Arnott. That made it the fourth-biggest wealth destroyer among mutual funds and ETFs in the ranking. 

Wood defended her investment strategy after an audience member at a recent summit questioned ARK's performance compared with the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ).

Related: Cathie Wood sells $16 million of surging tech stock

"Investors deserve to understand both their returns and the decisions behind them," Wood said in an Oct. 5 post on X.

She argued that the ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) and QQQ are built differently. QQQ tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index, while ARK actively invests in companies it believes are driving disruptive innovation across industries, including healthcare, financial services, and transportation.

Wood has long been optimistic about AI, which she sees as a major driver of productivity, economic growth, and corporate profits in the years ahead. She has also pushed back against recent fears that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

In September, Wood reposted a post by David Sacks on X, saying he makes a good case that the "AI will kill humanity" headlines were orchestrated.

title: Vistra Slides 17% in Three Months Despite a $4.2 Billion Nuclear Loan Offer
detail:
Vistra Slides 17% in Three Months Despite a $4.2 Billion Nuclear Loan Offer
Rexielyn Diaz
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 6:26 AM PDT 4 min read
VST
META
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Vistra Slides 17% in Three Months Despite a $4.2 Billion Nuclear Loan Offer ©Michael Pointner from Pexels and atlasstudio via Canva
Key Takeaways

Vistra closed at $140 on October 23, down 16.9% over three months, despite a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $4.2 billion.

The loan would fund 433 MW of uprates that Meta already contracted under 20-year PPAs covering 2,609 MW.

Q2 revenue missed badly at $4.02 billion, and management said power prices remain too low for new-build projects to earn adequate returns.

The November 6 Q3 report should update 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $6.8 billion to $7.6 billion and the Cogentrix closing timeline.

Good news has stopped moving Vistra (VST:NYSE). More precisely, it moves the stock for about a day.

In early October, the Energy Department offered up to $4.2 billion in conditional loans for Vistra's nuclear fleet. Shares rallied, then gave it all back and more. They closed at $140 on October 23, down 16.9% over three months and 31% below the $203.66 high.

Meanwhile, Vistra redeemed all of its Series A preferred stock for about $1 billion. Retail president Scott Hudson sold more than $10 million of shares across filings in September and October.

The market seems to be pricing something the headlines skip.

Washington offers cheap money

The Energy Department's Office of Energy Dominance Financing announced the conditional commitment on October 5. It covers uprates and modernization at Beaver Valley in Pennsylvania and at Davis-Besse and Perry in Ohio.

Those projects should preserve nearly 4 GW of existing nuclear output and add 433 MW of new capacity. An option also covers possible future uprates at Comanche Peak in Texas.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright framed the logic around "getting more power out of the nuclear plants we already have."

The catch sits in the word conditional. Vistra must still meet technical, legal, environmental and financial conditions before any money flows.

Debt is already climbing as Vistra funds growth…

Vistra (VST): total debt, $ billions, fiscal 2021–2025 (TIKR)

A fully drawn loan would add meaningfully to that total, so investors will watch how Vistra sizes the draw.

Meta already bought the megawatts

The loan matters because the output has a buyer. Vistra signed 20-year PPAs with Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) for 2,609 MW from Perry, Davis-Besse and Beaver Valley, including the 433 MW of planned uprates.

Deliveries start in late 2026, with full operating capacity by year-end 2027 and full uprate capacity by 2034.

At full delivery, those contracts should lift adjusted free cash flow before growth by 8% to 10% from existing energy. Uprates add another 5% to 7%.

Cogentrix adds the gas side. The roughly $4 billion deal brings 10 modern plants and about 5,500 MW, and it should close in mid-to-late 2026.

title: Why Are Investors Buying Credit Default Swaps to Hedge AI-Related Debt?
detail:
Why Are Investors Buying Credit Default Swaps to Hedge AI-Related Debt?

NVDA
ORCL
SPCX
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
What is driving increased demand for credit default swaps?

Investors are increasing their use of credit default swaps (CDS) to hedge exposure to debt issued by companies involved in artificial intelligence infrastructure, according to market data and financial industry research.

The increase comes as technology companies raise substantial amounts of capital to finance data centres, semiconductors and other computing infrastructure.

Morgan Stanley Research reported that weekly trading in CDS linked to bonds issued by Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Meta (NASDAQ:META), Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) averaged more than $9 billion in September.

That compares with less than $2 billion per week in July.

Separately, Bloomberg data showed that trading volumes in US corporate CDS indices have already exceeded the total recorded throughout 2025.

The increase reflects greater demand for instruments that can provide protection against credit losses or allow investors to express views on changes in corporate credit risk.

How much debt have AI-related companies issued in 2026?

According to Morgan Stanley, AI-linked debt issuance reached an estimated $466 billion so far in 2026, compared with $101 billion during the corresponding period of 2025.

The increase has been driven by financing requirements for artificial intelligence infrastructure, including data centres, chips and associated computing systems.

Companies involved in developing and operating these facilities have accessed bond markets and other credit sources to support their investment programmes.

The expansion in borrowing has also increased investor attention on the relationship between upfront capital expenditure and the revenue that infrastructure projects may generate over time.

As debt issuance grows, investors are assessing how financing costs, operating performance and the financial relationships between AI companies could affect creditworthiness.

How do credit default swaps work?

A credit default swap is a financial derivative that provides protection against specified credit events, such as a default by a corporate borrower.

The buyer of protection makes payments to the seller in exchange for compensation if a covered credit event occurs, subject to the contract's terms.

CDS prices are generally expressed as a spread in basis points, with 100 basis points equivalent to one percentage point annually.

For example, a CDS spread of 108 basis points represents an annual premium of approximately $108,000 to protect $10 million of debt, assuming a conventional running-premium structure.
